questions.question: Explain how `==` decides equality and why `===` is usually preferred.
questions.answer: `===` is strict: the types must match, then the values are compared, with no coercion. `==` first checks types; if they differ it coerces. `null` and `undefined` only equal each other, numbers and strings convert the string to a number, booleans convert to numbers, and objects convert to primitives via `ToPrimitive`. This produces surprises like `"0" == false` being true and `[] == false` being true, so `===` is preferred. The useful exception is `value == null`, which matches both `null` and `undefined`.
key_points: == converts booleans and strings to numbers
value == null checks both null and undefined

questions.question: What do `&&` and `||` actually return, and what does short-circuiting mean?
questions.answer: They return one of their operands, not necessarily a boolean. `&&` returns the first falsy operand or the last operand; `||` returns the first truthy operand or the last. Short-circuiting means evaluation stops as soon as the result is decided: the right side of `false && expensive()` never runs, and neither does the right side of `true || expensive()`. This is used for guards, defaults, and avoiding unnecessary work.
key_points: && returns first falsy or last operand
|| returns first truthy or last operand

questions.question: Predict: `console.log("10" < "9"); console.log("10" < 9); console.log(3 > 2 > 1);`
questions.answer: It prints `true`, `false`, `false`. Two strings compare lexicographically, so "1" comes before "9". When one side is a number, both convert to numbers, so 10 < 9 is false. The third parses left to right: `3 > 2` is `true`, then `true > 1` converts true to 1 and `1 > 1` is false.

questions.question: Why is `null >= 0` true but `null == 0` false?
questions.answer: They use different algorithms. Relational operators convert operands with `ToNumber`, and `Number(null)` is 0, so `0 >= 0` is true. Loose equality has a special rule: `null` only equals `undefined` and nothing else, so `null == 0` is false without any numeric conversion.

questions.question: How does `Object.is()` differ from `===`, and when would you use it?
questions.answer: `Object.is` behaves like `===` except for two cases: `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true while `NaN === NaN` is false, and `Object.is(0, -0)` is false while `0 === -0` is true. It is useful for same-value semantics such as React dependency checks, or when you must distinguish negative zero. It still compares objects by reference, not by contents.
key_points: Same as === except NaN and signed zero
